claim: 53BP1 and TOPBP1 are multi-domain scaffold proteins that individually contribute to the genome stability functions of mammalian cells.
source: 53BP1 and TOPBP1 are multi-domain scaffold proteins that individually contribute to the genome stability functions of mammalian cells (Sokka et al., 2010; Panier and Boulton, 2014; Wardlaw et al., 2014; Zimmermann and de Lange, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: 53BP1 is recruited to sites of DNA damage through interaction with post-translationally modified histones.
source: 53BP1 is recruited to sites of DNA damage through interaction with post-translationally modified histones (Botuyan et al., 2006; Fradet-Turcotte et al., 2013; Baldock et al., 2015; Kleiner et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: 53BP1 is strongly implicated in the process of choice between the non-homologous end joining and homologous recombination pathways of double-strand break (DSB) repair.
source: and is strongly implicated in the process of choice between the non-homologous end joining and homologous recombination pathways of double-strand break (DSB) repair (Leung and Glover, 2011; Aparicio et al., 2014; Daley and Sung, 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: 53BP1 is involved in the localisation of activated ATM that is required for DSB repair in heterochromatin.
source: as well as the localisation of activated ATM that is required for DSB repair in heterochromatin (Lee et al., 2010; Noon et al., 2010; Baldock et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: TOPBP1 is involved in replication initiation through its interaction with TICCR/Treslin.
source: Amongst other roles, TOPBP1 is involved in replication initiation through its interaction with TICCR/Treslin (Kumagai et al., 2010; Boos et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: TOPBP1 is involved in the DNA damage checkpoint through interactions with 9-1-1, RHNO1/RHINO and ATR.
source: the DNA damage checkpoint through interactions with 9-1-1, RHNO1/RHINO and ATR (Kumagai et al., 2006; Delacroix et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2007; Cotta-Ramusino et al., 2011; Lindsey-Boltz and Sancar, 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: TOPBP1 is involved in sister chromatid de-catenation and suppression of sister chromatid exchange via interactions with TOP2A and BLM.
source: and sister chromatid de-catenation and suppression of sister chromatid exchange via interactions with TOP2A and BLM (Blackford et al., 2015; Broderick et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The fission yeast orthologues of 53BP1 and TOPBP1 are Crb2 and Rad4 (also known as Cut5) respectively.
source: Genetic studies indicate that the fission yeast orthologues of 53BP1 and TOPBP1 – Crb2 and Rad4 (also known as Cut5) respectively – interact directly with each other, and play important roles in the DNA damage response (Saka et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Crb2 and Rad4 interact directly with each other and play important roles in the DNA damage response.
source: Genetic studies indicate that the fission yeast orthologues of 53BP1 and TOPBP1 – Crb2 and Rad4 (also known as Cut5) respectively – interact directly with each other, and play important roles in the DNA damage response (Saka et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Physical association of Crb2 and Rad4 is mediated by the interaction of a pattern of cyclin-dependent kinase phosphorylation sites on Crb2, with the BRCT domains of Rad4.
source: Subsequent studies have shown that physical association of Crb2 and Rad4 is mediated by the interaction of a pattern of cyclin-dependent kinase phosphorylation sites on Crb2, with the BRCT domains of Rad4 (Du et al., 2006; Qu et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A functionally important physical interaction of mammalian 53BP1 and TOPBP1 has been observed.
source: A functionally important physical interaction of mammalian 53BP1 and TOPBP1 has also been observed (Cescutti et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The interaction of mammalian 53BP1 and TOPBP1 depends upon the functionality of specific TOPBP1 BRCT domains.
source: and found to depend upon the functionality of specific TOPBP1 BRCT domains, suggesting that this interaction might also mediated by phosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Cescutti et al., 2010) in the preceding sentence.

claim: Four potential TOPBP1-binding phosphorylation sites in 53BP1 were identified using a structurally-derived consensus pattern, focused on Thr334, Ser366, Ser380 and Thr670.
source: Using a consensus motif for selective phosphopeptide-binding to BRCT domains of TOPBP1/Rad4 (Day et al., 2018), we searched for potential phosphorylation sites in 53BP1 that might be involved in mediating phosphorylation-dependent interactions with TOPBP1. Four matches were identified, focused on Thr334, Ser366, Ser380 and Thr670
evidence: The claim is based on computational analysis using a consensus motif and is shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Thr334, Ser366, Ser380 and Thr670 of 53BP1 have been previously documented as phosphorylated in phospho-proteomic analyses.
source: all of which have been previously documented as phosphorylated in phospho-proteomic analyses (Hornbeck et al., 2004; Sharma et al., 2014) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior phospho-proteomic studies and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Ser380 of 53BP1 has been previously implicated in binding the pro-homology repair factor SCAI.
source: While Ser380 has previously been implicated in binding the pro-homology repair factor SCAI (Isobe et al., 2017), no function has been assigned to the other sites we identified.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: A fluorescently labelled phospho-peptide centred on 53BP1-Thr670 binds to the BRCT0,1,2 segment of TOPBP1 with high affinity (Kd = 1.5 ± 0.2 μM).
source: Of the four peptides, only the one centred on 53BP1-pThr670 bound tightly to TOPBP1-BRCT0,1,2 (Kd = 1.5 ± 0.2 μM) (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is based on fluorescence polarisation measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Treatment with λ-phosphatase eliminates binding of the 53BP1-pThr670 peptide to TOPBP1-BRCT0,1,2, confirming that phosphorylation of the 53BP1 sequence is required.
source: Treatment with λ-phosphatase eliminated binding, confirming that phosphorylation of the 53BP1 sequence is required (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: BRCT2 is the primary binding site for the 53BP1-pThr670 peptide within TOPBP1-BRCT0,1,2.
source: These data implicate BRCT2 as the primary binding site, consistent with the presence of a hydrophilic residue −4 to the phosphothreonine (Day et al., 2018), but with BRCT1 potentially providing a weaker alternative site.
evidence: The claim is based on mutagenesis data shown in Figure 1D and inference from the binding pattern.

claim: Mutation of both BRCT1 and BRCT2 phospho-binding sites in TOPBP1 eliminated interaction with the 53BP1-pThr670 peptide.
source: Mutation of both BRCT phospho-binding sites eliminated interaction (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The 53BP1-pSer366 peptide binds to TOPBP1-BRCT4,5 with modest affinity (Kd = 20.6 ± 1.9 μM).
source: However, the 53BP1-pSer366 peptide did show a clear interaction with TOPBP1-BRCT4,5, albeit with a more modest affinity (Kd = 20.6 ± 1.9 μM).
evidence: The claim is based on fluorescence polarisation measurements shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The 53BP1-pSer380 peptide binds to TOPBP1-BRCT4,5 with lower affinity (Kd = 29.6 ± 2.6 μM).
source: 53BP1-pSer380 also bound TOPBP1-BRCT4,5 but with still lower affinity (Kd = 29.6 ± 2.6 μM) (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is based on fluorescence polarisation measurements shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Treatment of the 53BP1-pSer366 phosphopeptide with λ-phosphatase eliminates binding to TOPBP1-BRCT4,5, confirming the phospho-specificity of the interaction.
source: Treatment of the phosphopeptide with λ-phosphatase or mutation of Lys704, which is implicated in phosphate recognition in TOPBP1-BRCT4,5 eliminated binding, confirming the phospho-specificity of the interaction (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Mutation of Lys704 in TOPBP1-BRCT4,5 eliminates binding of the 53BP1-pSer366 phosphopeptide, confirming the phospho-specificity of the interaction.
source: Treatment of the phosphopeptide with λ-phosphatase or mutation of Lys704, which is implicated in phosphate recognition in TOPBP1-BRCT4,5 eliminated binding, confirming the phospho-specificity of the interaction (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The 53BP1-pThr670 peptide binds to BRCT2 of TOPBP1.
source: Co-crystallisation of TOPBP1-BRCT0,1,2 with the 53BP1-pThr670 phospho-peptide produced a crystal structure with peptide bound to BRCT2, consistent with the specificity it displays for that site in binding assays (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is based on crystal structure data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The position and overall conformation of the 53BP1-pThr670 peptide bound to TOPBP1-BRCT2 is similar to that previously described for the interaction of Crb2-derived phospho-peptides pThr187 and pThr235 bound to BRCT2 of Rad4.
source: The position and overall conformation of the bound peptide is similar to that previously described for the interaction of Crb2-derived phospho-peptides pThr187 and pThr235 bound to BRCT2 of Rad4 (Qu et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with prior structural data.

claim: The phosphorylated side chain of 53BP1-Thr670 interacts with TOPBP1-Thr208 and TOPBP1-Lys250.
source: The phosphorylated side chain of 53BP1-Thr670 interacts with TOPBP1-Thr208 and TOPBP1-Lys250, which are topologically conserved in all BRCT domains capable of phospho-specific peptide interaction (Leung and Glover, 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on structural data shown in Figure 2B and comparison with conserved features.

claim: The 53BP1-pSer366 peptide binds to BRCT5 of TOPBP1.
source: The 53BP1-pSer366 peptide binds to BRCT5 in a similar position and orientation as previously observed for phospho-peptide binding to TOPBP1-BRCT1 and BRCT2 (see above) and Rad4-BRCT1 and BRCT2 (Qu et al., 2013) (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is based on crystal structure data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: The mode of binding of the 53BP1-pSer366 peptide to TOPBP1-BRCT5 is markedly different from that reported for binding of an MDC1-derived phospho-peptide to TOPBP1-BRCT4,5.
source: This mode of binding, conserved in Rad4 and N-terminal TOPBP1 BRCT domain interactions, is markedly different from that reported for binding of an MDC1-derived phospho-peptide to TOPBP1-BRCT4,5 (Leung et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with prior structural data.

claim: TOPBP1-BRCT4,5 has been identified as the binding site for a phosphorylated motif in the RECQ-family helicase BLM.
source: Interestingly, TOPBP1-BRCT4,5 has recently been identified as the binding site for a phosphorylated motif in the RECQ-family helicase BLM (Blackford et al., 2015) and a crystal structure of the complex determined (Sun et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The identified binding site in BLM (300-FVPPpSPE-306) shows strong similarity to the 53BP1-motif (362-LVAPpSPD-368).
source: The identified binding site in BLM - 300-FVPPpSPE-306 shows strong similarity to the 53BP1-motif we have identified - 362-LVAPpSPD-368, and binds to BRCT5 in a very similar manner
evidence: The claim is based on sequence comparison and structural similarity.

claim: The binding mode of the BLM phosphopeptide to TOPBP1-BRCT5 is quite different from the proposed binding mode of the MDC1 SDT motif.
source: but quite differently from the proposed binding mode of the MDC1 SDT motif (Leung et al., 2013), which we have recently shown plays no role in mediating MDC1 interaction with TOPBP1 (Leimbacher et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on structural comparison and recent experimental findings.

claim: Clear reactive bands for 53BP1-pSer366 and 53BP1-pThr670 were seen in HeLa cell lysates following ionising radiation.
source: For both α−53BP1-pSer366 and α−53BP1-pThr670 antibodies, clear reactive bands were seen following IR, which were weaker in non-irradiated cells, and considerably diminished by siRNA knockdown of 53BP1 (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is based on western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: siRNA knockdown of 53BP1 considerably diminished the reactive bands for 53BP1-pSer366 and 53BP1-pThr670 antibodies in HeLa cell lysates.
source: For both α−53BP1-pSer366 and α−53BP1-pThr670 antibodies, clear reactive bands were seen following IR, which were weaker in non-irradiated cells, and considerably diminished by siRNA knockdown of 53BP1 (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is based on western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 53BP1-pSer366 and 53BP1-pThr670 immunofluorescence foci co-localise with eYFP-53BP1 in irradiated U2OS cells.
source: We also performed immunofluorescence with these antibodies in irradiated U2OS cells (Figure 3B) and observed strong co-localisation of foci formed by the phospho-specific antibodies with those formed by antibodies to total 53BP1, consistent with the endogenous protein being phosphorylated on Ser366 and Thr670.
evidence: The claim is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The eYFP signal coincides with immunofluorescent foci to total 53BP1 in wild-type constructs, but this coincidence is lost for both phospho-specific antibodies in cells transfected with 53BP1 mutated in their respective phosphorylation site epitope.
source: While we saw strong coincidence of the eYFP signal with immunofluorescent foci to total 53BP1 in the wild-type constructs, this was lost for both of the phospho-specific antibodies in cells transfected with 53BP1 mutated in their respective phosphorylation site epitope (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: TOPBP1 and eYFP-53BP1 co-localise into damage foci in G1 U2OS cells following irradiation.
source: In both cell types expressing tagged wild-type eYFP-53BP1 constructs, TOPBP1 and eYFP-53BP1 co-localised into damage foci in G1 (Cyclin A negative) cells following irradiation, reflecting the direct interactions we observed in vitro.
evidence: The claim is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Formation of TOPBP1 foci coincident with eYFP-53BP1 foci is significantly reduced in irradiated U2OS cells expressing the 53BP1-S366A and/or T670A mutants.
source: However, while irradiated U2OS cells expressing the 53BP1-S366A and/or T670A mutants, still formed eYFP-53BP1 foci, formation of TOPBP1 foci coincident with these was significantly reduced (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: The claim is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A and statistical analysis in Figure 4B.

claim: A very similar effect on TOPBP1 foci formation was seen in RPE1 cells expressing 53BP1-S366A and/or T670A mutants.
source: A very similar effect was seen in RPE1 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Both Ser366 and Thr670 phosphorylation sites are required for maintaining the interaction between 53BP1 and TOPBP1 and for recruiting TOPBP1 into 53BP1 damage foci in G1 cells.
source: These data suggest that both of these phosphorylation sites are required for maintaining the interaction between 53BP1 and TOPBP1 and for recruiting TOPBP1 into 53BP1 damage foci in G1 cells negative for cyclin A.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the immunofluorescence data showing reduced TOPBP1 foci formation in mutants.

claim: Wild-type U2OS cells show a G1/S checkpoint in response to ionising radiation.
source: Wild-type U2OS and RPE1 cells both showed a G1/S checkpoint in response to ionising radiation (IR), with few cells moving into DNA synthesis (visualised by BrdU incorporation) as compared to untreated cells.
evidence: The claim is based on checkpoint assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The G1/S checkpoint in response to ionising radiation is greatly reduced in U2OS cells in which 53BP1 protein levels were knocked down by siRNA.
source: However, this G1/S checkpoint was greatly reduced in cells of either type in which 53BP1 protein levels were knocked down by siRNA, confirming a critical role for 53BP1 (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is based on checkpoint assay data shown in Figure 4C and supplementary figures.

claim: The checkpoint response to ionising radiation in U2OS cells is largely restored in 53BP1 knockdown cells by expression of an siRNA-resistant 53BP1 construct, but not by 53BP1 constructs with S366A and/or T670A mutations.
source: The checkpoint response to IR in both cell types was largely restored in the 53BP1 knockdown cells by expression of an siRNA-resistant 53BP1 construct, but not by 53BP1 constructs with S366A and/or T670A mutations (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is based on checkpoint assay data shown in Figure 4D and supplementary figures.

claim: The cell cycle distribution of irradiated U2OS cells expressing the S366A or T670A mutants were significantly perturbed compared with wild-type, with the mutants displaying fewer cells in G1 or S phases and a higher proportion in G2.
source: Consistent with this, we found that the cell cycle distribution of irradiated U2OS cells expressing the mutants were significantly perturbed compared with wild-type, with the mutants displaying fewer cells in G1 or S phases and a higher proportion in G2 (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is based on cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: ATM and ATR form nuclear foci in G1 cells following irradiation.
source: ATM and ATR have both been previously shown to form nuclear foci in G1 cells following irradiation (for example Adams et al., 2006; Noon et al., 2010; Gamper et al., 2013; Averbeck et al., 2014; Baldock et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: pATM and pATR display distinct immunofluorescent foci that co-localise with 53BP1 and TOPBP1 in irradiated G1 U2OS cells expressing wild-type eYFP-53BP1.
source: Using validated phospho-specific antibodies to the activated states of the proteins (Noon et al., 2010 and Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2) we found that both pATM and pATR display distinct immunofluorescent foci that co-localise with 53BP1 and TOPBP1 in irradiated G1 U2OS cells expressing wild-type eYFP-53BP1.
evidence: The claim is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5 and supplementary figures.

claim: Mutation of Ser366 and/or Thr670 in 53BP1 had no significant effect on pATM focus formation and co-localisation with 53BP1 in U2OS or RPE1 cells in G1.
source: Unlike 53BP1 knockdown or point mutations in the C-terminal tandem BRCT domain of 53BP1 that affect its interaction with γH2AX (Baldock et al., 2015) mutation of Ser366 and/or Thr670 had no significant effect on pATM focus formation and co-localisation with 53BP1 in U2OS or RPE1 cells in G1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: TOPBP1 plays no significant role in ATM activation or localisation.
source: This suggests that TOPBP1, which no longer co-localises with 53BP1 bearing S366A and/or T670A mutations, plays no significant role in ATM activation or localisation.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that pATM foci are unaffected by mutations that disrupt TOPBP1-53BP1 interaction.

claim: Co-localisation of pATR foci with 53BP1 was significantly disrupted by the S366A and/or T670A mutations of 53BP1.
source: In marked contrast, co-localisation of pATR foci with 53BP1 was significantly disrupted (Figure 5A,B) by the S366A and/or T670A mutations of 53BP1.
evidence: The claim is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A and statistical analysis in Figure 5B.

claim: CHK1 forms nuclear foci following irradiation.
source: CHK1, which is activated by ATR in the DNA damage checkpoint response, has also been previously shown to form nuclear foci following irradiation (Peddibhotla et al., 2011; Burdak-Rothkamm et al., 2015; Antonczak et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CHK1 foci co-incident with wild-type eYFP-53BP1 were observed in 53BP1-knockdown G1 RPE1 cells following irradiation.
source: Using antibodies to total CHK1, we also observed distinct CHK1 foci co-incident with wild-type eYFP-53BP1 in 53BP1-knockdown G1 RPE1 cells following irradiation
evidence: The claim is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: CHK1 displayed a diffuse pan-nuclear distribution in irradiated cells in which 53BP1 was knocked down by siRNA.
source: but not in irradiated cells in which 53BP1 was knocked down by siRNA, where CHK1 displayed a diffuse pan-nuclear distribution (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: CHK1 foci were restored in 53BP1 knockdown cells expressing siRNA-resistant wild-type eYFP-53BP1, but not in cells expressing eYFP-53BP1 with S366A and/or T670A mutations.
source: CHK1 foci were restored in 53BP1 knockdown cells expressing siRNA-resistant wild-type eYFP-53BP1, but not in cells expressing eYFP-53BP1 with S366A and/or T670A mutations, which displayed the same diffuse distribution of CHK1 as the 53BP1 knockdown cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Recruitment of CHK1 to sites of DNA damage in G1 and its activating interaction with ATR is dependent on the 53BP1-TOPBP1 interaction.
source: While CHK1, unlike ATR, is not a direct ligand of TOPBP1, these data suggest that its recruitment to sites of DNA damage in G1 and its activating interaction with ATR, most likely mediated by claspin (Liu et al., 2006), is dependent on the 53BP1-TOPBP1 interaction.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the immunofluorescence data and prior knowledge about CHK1 activation.

claim: Significant decreases in DNA damage induced TP53-Ser15 phosphorylation were observed in 53BP1 knockdown G1 U2OS cells expressing S366A or T670A eYFP-53BP1, compared to wild-type.
source: Consistent with this functional disruption of ATR and CHK1, we observed significant decreases in DNA damage induced TP53-Ser15 phosphorylation (Shieh et al., 2000; Helt et al., 2005) and total TP53 and p21 levels, in 53BP1 knockdown G1 U2OS cells expressing S366A or T670A eYFP-53BP1, compared to wild-type (Figure 5E,F,G,H).
evidence: The claim is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5E-H.

claim: Significant decreases in total TP53 and p21 levels were observed in 53BP1 knockdown G1 U2OS cells expressing S366A or T670A eYFP-53BP1, compared to wild-type.
source: Consistent with this functional disruption of ATR and CHK1, we observed significant decreases in DNA damage induced TP53-Ser15 phosphorylation (Shieh et al., 2000; Helt et al., 2005) and total TP53 and p21 levels, in 53BP1 knockdown G1 U2OS cells expressing S366A or T670A eYFP-53BP1, compared to wild-type (Figure 5E,F,G,H).
evidence: The claim is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5E-H.

claim: ATR localisation to DNA damage sites in S and G2 phases requires interaction of its constitutive partner, ATRIP, with RPA-bound segments of ssDNA.
source: ATR localisation to DNA damage sites in S and G2 phases, requires interaction of its constitutive partner, ATRIP, with RPA-bound segments of ssDNA, arising through replication fork collapse, or resection of DSBs by MRN as a prelude to repair by HR (Maréchal and Zou, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Activation of ATR requires interaction with the AAD-domain of TOPBP1.
source: Activation of ATR additionally requires interaction with the AAD-domain of TOPBP1, which is recruited to damage sites via interaction with the phosphorylated C-terminus of RAD9 (Lee et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: TOPBP1 is recruited to damage sites via interaction with the phosphorylated C-terminus of RAD9 within the RAD9-RAD1-HUS1 (9-1-1) checkpoint clamp.
source: which is recruited to damage sites via interaction with the phosphorylated C-terminus of RAD9 (Lee et al., 2007), within the toroidal RAD9-RAD1-HUS1 (9-1-1) checkpoint clamp (Doré et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The 9-1-1 checkpoint clamp is loaded at the inner margin of the ssDNA segment by the RAD17-RFC clamp loader complex.
source: itself loaded at the inner margin of the ssDNA segment by the RAD17-RFC clamp loader complex (Ohashi and Tsurimoto, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The critical phosphorylation sites on 53BP1 selectively interact with BRCT domains 2 and 5 of TOPBP1.
source: As our biochemical and structural analysis shows that the critical phosphorylation sites on 53BP1 selectively interact with BRCT domains 2 and 5 of TOPBP1
evidence: The claim is based on the biochemical and structural data presented earlier in the manuscript.

claim: Binding of 53BP1 to a TOPBP1 molecule would not in principle preclude simultaneous binding of the RAD9-tail, which is strongly selective for BRCT1.
source: binding of 53BP1 to a TOPBP1 molecule would not in principle preclude simultaneous binding of the RAD9-tail, which is strongly selective for BRCT1 (Rappas et al., 2011; Day et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the structural data and prior knowledge of RAD9 binding specificity.

claim: 53BP1 and RAD9 immunofluorescence foci partially co-localise in irradiated RPE1 cells.
source: we looked at the distributions of 53BP1 and 9-1-1 (via RAD9) in the nuclei of irradiated G1 RPE1 cells, and observed substantial coincidence of 53BP1 and RAD9 foci (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A strong PLA signal between RAD9 and 53BP1 was observed in irradiated cells.
source: We observed a strong PLA signal between RAD9 and 53BP1 in irradiated cells (Figure 6C)
evidence: The claim is based on proximity ligation assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The PLA signal between RAD9 and 53BP1 increased significantly on exposure to ionising radiation.
source: which increased significantly on exposure to IR (Figure 6D,E)
evidence: The claim is based on proximity ligation assay data shown in Figure 6D and statistical analysis in Figure 6E.

claim: The major effect of the PLA signal increase occurred in cells featuring the lowest Hoechst intensity typical of G1 cells with low DNA content.
source: with the major effect occurring in cells featuring the lowest Hoechst intensity typical of G1 cells with low DNA content.
evidence: The claim is based on proximity ligation assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: A significant loss of the proximity signal between RAD9 and 53BP1 was observed in irradiated cells when TOPBP1 levels were knocked down by siRNA.
source: When TOPBP1 levels were knocked down by siRNA, we observed a significant loss of the proximity signal between RAD9 and 53BP1 in irradiated cells (Figure 6F)
evidence: The claim is based on proximity ligation assay data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: TOPBP1 plays a pivotal role in bringing RAD9 and 53BP1 into proximity.
source: consistent with TOPBP1 playing a pivotal role in bringing these two damage recognition proteins into proximity.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the PLA data showing loss of proximity signal when TOPBP1 is knocked down.

claim: The RAD9-eYFP PLA signal was significantly diminished when cells were transfected with eYFP-53BP1 constructs with S366A and T670A mutations.
source: However, consistent with the role of pSer366 and pThr670 in mediating recruitment of the eYFP-53BP1 to TOPBP1 and thereby bringing it into close proximity to RAD9, the RAD9-eYFP PLA signal was significantly diminished when the cells were transfected with eYFP-53BP1 constructs with S366A and T670A mutations (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is based on proximity ligation assay data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: 53BP1 is a highly post-translationally modified protein, with more than 200 phosphorylation sites documented in the human protein.
source: 53BP1 is a highly post-translationally modified protein, with more than 200 phosphorylation sites documented in the human protein (Hornbeck et al., 2004)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a phosphorylation database.

claim: Only a handful of the more than 200 phosphorylation sites in 53BP1 have been associated with any biological function.
source: of which only a handful have been associated with any biological function (Panier and Boulton, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: The major interacting sites Ser366 and Thr670 are strongly conserved in metazoa.
source: The major interacting sites, Ser366 and Thr670, are strongly conserved in metazoa
evidence: The claim is based on sequence conservation analysis.

claim: Ser366 and Thr670 of 53BP1 are found to be phosphorylated in human, mouse and rat cells.
source: and found to be phosphorylated in human, mouse and rat cells (Hornbeck et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a phosphorylation database.

claim: Phosphorylation of Ser366 and Thr670 in 53BP1 is enhanced in response to DNA damage.
source: Although these SP/TP sites resemble typical CDK substrates, we find that their phosphorylation is enhanced in response to DNA damage
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations in the study.

claim: Phosphorylation of Ser366 and Thr670 in 53BP1 is not prevented by a broad range of CDK kinase inhibitors.
source: and is not prevented by a broad range of CDK kinase inhibitors (data not shown) suggesting that they are not under cell cycle control.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations (data not shown).

claim: Phosphorylation of the sites mediating Crb2 and Rad9p interaction with Rad4 and Dpb11p in fission and budding yeasts are under CDK-dependent cell cycle regulation.
source: This contrasts with fission and budding yeasts, where phosphorylation of the sites mediating Crb2 and Rad9p interaction with Rad4 and Dpb11p are under CDK-dependent cell cycle regulation (Du et al., 2006; Pfander and Diffley, 2011; Qu et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A recent study identifies a DNA damage-dependent and cell cycle-independent pathway for phosphorylation of the sites mediating interaction of budding yeast Rad9p with Dpb11p.
source: However, a recent study also identifies a DNA damage-dependent and cell cycle-independent pathway for phosphorylation of the sites mediating interaction of budding yeast Rad9p with Dpb11p (di Cicco et al., 2017), which may be comparable to that we describe here for the human proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to recent research.

claim: The strongest effects on the DNA damage response are seen when neither Ser366 nor Thr670 can be phosphorylated.
source: Although mutation of either Ser366 or Thr670 impacts on the DNA damage response, the strongest effects are seen when neither site can be phosphorylated.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations throughout the study.
